subject: history

questions.content: Which title was held by Nicholas II, who ruled Russia from 1894 until 1917?
options: Kaiser
Tsar and autocrat
Chancellor
President of the Duma
questions.explanation: Nicholas II was the Tsar, an autocrat who claimed to rule with no parliament limiting his power. 'Kaiser' was the German emperor's title.

questions.content: About what proportion of the Russian population were peasants around 1900?
options: About 20%
About 50%
About 95%
About 80%
questions.explanation: Russia was overwhelmingly rural, with roughly four in five people living as peasants. This is why land hunger and rural poverty mattered so much.

questions.content: What happened on Bloody Sunday, 22 January 1905?
options: Troops fired on a peaceful march led by Father Gapon that was taking a petition to the Tsar
The Tsar abdicated in favour of his brother
Sailors on the battleship Potemkin mutinied
Bolsheviks stormed the Winter Palace
questions.explanation: Soldiers shot at unarmed workers and their families, which destroyed much of the faith they had in the Tsar. The Potemkin mutiny came later in 1905.

questions.content: Which war's defeats in 1904–05 damaged the Tsar's prestige and helped spark the 1905 Revolution?
options: The Crimean War
The Franco-Prussian War
The Russo-Japanese War
The Boer War
questions.explanation: Russia lost battles such as Port Arthur and Tsushima to Japan. The Crimean War was fought in 1853–56, far earlier.

questions.content: What did the October Manifesto of 1905 promise?
options: An end to the monarchy
An elected Duma and civil liberties
Free land for every peasant
Russia's withdrawal from the war with Japan
questions.explanation: Nicholas II issued it under pressure to calm the revolution, promising an elected parliament (the Duma) and freedoms such as speech and assembly.

questions.content: An invented report from a visitor to Petrograd in 1903 says: 'A family of six shares one damp room. Wages are low, hours are long, and a complaint can mean dismissal.' Which cause of unrest does it best illustrate?
options: Poor conditions for the new industrial working class
Religious persecution by the Orthodox Church
Military defeat by Germany
The weakness of the Duma
questions.explanation: The extract describes housing, pay and hours in a city, which are typical complaints of industrial workers. The Duma did not yet exist in 1903.

questions.content: Why did Stolypin's land reforms aim to create prosperous peasant farmers (kulaks)?
options: To prepare for collective farming
To give land to workers' councils
To reduce the size of the army
To build a loyal, conservative class who would support the Tsar
questions.explanation: Stolypin hoped that peasants who owned their land would have a stake in the system and not turn to revolution. Collectivisation was a later Soviet policy.

questions.content: Which group, formed after the 1903 split, followed Lenin's plan for a small, disciplined party of professional revolutionaries?
options: The Mensheviks
The Kadets
The Bolsheviks
The Social Revolutionaries
questions.explanation: The Social Democrats split in 1903. Lenin's supporters were the Bolsheviks; the Mensheviks wanted a broader membership.

questions.content: Why did the Fundamental Laws of 1906 weaken the promise of the October Manifesto?
options: They abolished the Duma
They kept the Tsar's power to choose ministers, veto laws and dissolve the Duma
They gave the Duma control of the army
They banned all political parties
questions.explanation: The Tsar kept real power and could ignore or dissolve the Duma, so many reformers felt that the Manifesto had been only a partial concession.

questions.content: In September 1915 Nicholas II took personal command of the army. Why was this a political mistake?
options: Military defeats could now be blamed directly on him, and he left the government in Petrograd under Alexandra and Rasputin's influence
It meant he had to sign a peace treaty
It gave the Duma control of the war
It removed the army's best generals
questions.explanation: As commander he was personally linked to defeats, and with him away from the capital, the unpopular Tsarina and Rasputin were seen to be influencing appointments.

questions.content: Why did Rasputin damage the reputation of the monarchy?
options: He led the first Duma
He organised strikes in Petrograd
Rumour said he controlled the Tsarina and government appointments
He joined the Bolsheviks
questions.explanation: Rasputin's influence over Alexandra, who relied on him partly because of her son Alexei's haemophilia, led to scandal and loss of respect for the royal family.

questions.content: Which is a long-term cause rather than a short-term trigger of the 1917 revolutions?
options: Bread shortages in Petrograd in winter 1916–17
Military defeats in 1915–16
The Tsar's absence at the front from 1915
The Tsars' long-standing refusal to share power
questions.explanation: Autocracy had existed for centuries and prevented reform. The other options all belong to the First World War period, which is short-term.

questions.content: What was the role of the Okhrana?
options: An elected council of peasants
Tsarist secret police that spied on and arrested opponents
The Bolsheviks' armed wing
A committee of the Orthodox Church
questions.explanation: The Okhrana infiltrated revolutionary groups, censored publications and arrested suspects, one way the autocracy controlled opposition.

questions.content: Which evidence best supports the view that the Tsarist regime was already unstable BEFORE the First World War began?
options: Strikes rose sharply in 1912–14 after the shooting of miners in the Lena goldfields
The defeat at Tannenberg in August 1914
Bread shortages in Petrograd in 1917
The Tsar's abdication in March 1917
questions.explanation: Rising industrial unrest in 1912–14 predates the war. The other options all happened during or after the war began.

questions.content: An invented 1905 report from a regional official says: 'The disturbance was the work of a few agitators; the ordinary people remain loyal.' What is the main limitation of this source for studying the 1905 Revolution?
options: It is useless because officials never write accurately
It is reliable because it was written at the time
The author had a reason to play down unrest to protect his own position and the regime
It cannot be used because it was written in Russia
questions.explanation: Officials had a motive to reassure their superiors, so the report may understate the unrest. It is still valuable for showing how the regime wished to see events.

questions.content: Why was rapid industrialisation under Witte both a success and a source of instability?
options: It ended the power of the Okhrana
It made peasants wealthy enough to support the Tsar
It removed the need for foreign loans
It created growth but also a large, discontented working class in crowded cities
questions.explanation: Factories produced economic growth, but the new workers faced poor conditions and were open to revolutionary ideas, which increased the danger to the regime.

questions.content: Which statement is the most balanced judgement of Stolypin?
options: He combined repression and reform to strengthen the regime but was assassinated in 1911 before his reforms could show full results
He was a liberal who wanted to end autocracy
He abolished the Duma and ruled alone
He fully succeeded, proving that rural problems were not a cause of revolution
questions.explanation: Stolypin used hangings and land reform together; his death in 1911 and the limited time to work make it hard to say whether reform could have saved the regime.

questions.content: Why did Nicholas II survive the 1905 Revolution?
options: The Duma defended him
Revolutionary parties were united behind a plan
The army stayed largely loyal and the October Manifesto divided his opponents
Japan helped him to crush the strikes
questions.explanation: Concessions satisfied the moderates while loyal troops put down the more radical risings, so the opposition could not unite.

note:
## An autocracy under strain
In 1900 Russia was the largest country in the world and an autocracy: Tsar Nicholas II (ruled 1894–1917) held all political power and answered to no parliament. He was supported by the Orthodox Church, the nobility, the army and the Okhrana, the secret police that spied on opponents. About 80% of Russians were peasants living in villages, often on tiny plots, and many suffered poverty and land hunger even though serfdom had ended in 1861.

## Industrialisation and discontent
Under ministers such as Sergei Witte, Russia industrialised quickly in the 1890s, helped by foreign loans and projects like the Trans-Siberian Railway. Factories in St Petersburg (renamed Petrograd in 1914) and Moscow grew fast. The new industrial working class faced long hours, low pay, dangerous work and cramped housing. Strikes were illegal, and many workers were attracted to revolutionary ideas.

## Opposition groups
- **Social Revolutionaries (SRs)**: wanted land for the peasants and sometimes used terrorism against officials.
- **Social Democrats**: Marxists who split in 1903 into **Bolsheviks** (led by Lenin, wanting a small, disciplined party of full-time revolutionaries) and **Mensheviks** (wanting a wider membership).
- **Kadets**: liberals who wanted a constitutional monarchy.

## The 1905 Revolution
Russia lost the Russo-Japanese War (1904–05), including humiliating defeats at Port Arthur and Tsushima. On **Bloody Sunday, 22 January 1905**, troops fired on a peaceful march led by Father Gapon, who was carrying a petition to the Tsar at the Winter Palace. Strikes, peasant risings and mutinies (such as on the battleship Potemkin) followed. Nicholas survived by issuing the **October Manifesto**, promising an elected Duma and civil liberties, which split his opponents. The army stayed largely loyal. Afterwards the Fundamental Laws of 1906 kept the Tsar's power to choose ministers, veto laws and dissolve the Duma.

## Reform and repression: Stolypin
Pyotr Stolypin, Prime Minister from 1906 until he was assassinated in 1911, combined harsh repression (the hangings nicknamed 'Stolypin's necktie') with land reforms meant to create prosperous, conservative peasant farmers, called kulaks. His reforms had little time to work.

## The First World War
War in 1914 brought huge defeats (such as Tannenberg), millions of casualties, shortages and inflation. In September 1915 Nicholas took personal command of the army, so defeats became his responsibility. In the capital, the Tsarina Alexandra, unpopular for her German birth, relied on the monk Rasputin, who was widely believed to influence appointments. Rasputin was murdered in December 1916 by a group of nobles.

## Common mistakes
- Do not say the Tsar's regime collapsed in 1905; it survived.
- Do not treat the war as the only cause. Historians separate long-term causes (autocracy, poverty), medium-term causes (1905, limited reform) and short-term triggers (war, food shortages).

## How this is examined
Expect a short source (a report, a poster, a photograph description) from before 1917 with a command term such as 'explain', 'compare' or 'evaluate'. You may need to state the origin and purpose of the source, use it with your own knowledge to explain why the regime was unstable, and judge which cause was most important with a justified reason.

Exam tip: when asked 'how far' the Tsar caused his own downfall, balance his weaknesses (refusing to share power, taking command of the army) against other factors such as the war and wider social pressures, then reach a clear judgement.

flashcards.back: Rule by one person with unlimited power. Nicholas II was an autocrat who did not share power with an elected parliament until forced to in 1905.
The Tsar's secret police, which spied on, arrested and exiled opponents of the regime.
22 January 1905: troops fired on a peaceful march led by Father Gapon to the Winter Palace. It destroyed trust in the Tsar and began the 1905 Revolution.
Promise by Nicholas II of an elected Duma and civil liberties. It divided his opponents and helped him survive the revolution.
Laws that kept the Tsar's power to appoint ministers, veto laws and dissolve the Duma, limiting the reforms of 1905.
The two wings of the Social Democrats after 1903. Bolsheviks (Lenin): small disciplined party. Mensheviks: broader membership.
Prime Minister 1906–1911. Used harsh repression and land reforms to create loyal kulaks. Assassinated in 1911.
Minister who drove Russian industrialisation in the 1890s with foreign loans and railways, creating a discontented urban working class.

flashcards.front: Why the war weakened the Tsar
flashcards.back: Defeats, casualties and shortages; the Tsar took command of the army in 1915 and was blamed; Rasputin's influence harmed the royal family's reputation.

subject: history

questions.content: Which event sparked the February Revolution of 1917 in Petrograd?
options: The assassination of the Tsar
A Bolshevik attack on the Winter Palace
Strikes and protests over bread shortages, beginning on International Women's Day
A German invasion of Petrograd
questions.explanation: Women textile workers and others protested over food shortages on 23 February (Old Style), and strikes spread until soldiers joined the crowds.

questions.content: Who held power in Russia after Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917?
options: A Provisional Government
The Bolshevik party under Lenin
The Tsar's brother Michael as Tsar
The Constituent Assembly
questions.explanation: Michael declined the throne, and the Duma's leaders formed a Provisional Government that shared authority with the Petrograd Soviet.

questions.content: Which slogan summarised Lenin's April Theses?
options: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity
Peace, Land and Bread
Autocracy, Orthodoxy, Nationality
Work, Faith, Family
questions.explanation: Lenin promised an end to the war, land for peasants and food for workers, a simple message with wide appeal.

questions.content: Who organised the Bolshevik seizure of power in October 1917 through the Petrograd Soviet's Military Revolutionary Committee?
options: Kerensky
Kornilov
Stalin
Trotsky
questions.explanation: Trotsky, not Lenin, planned the practical details of the takeover, while Lenin pressed the party to act.

questions.content: Which building in Petrograd did Bolshevik forces storm in October 1917?
options: The Kremlin
The Tauride Palace
The Winter Palace
The Peter and Paul Fortress
questions.explanation: The Winter Palace was where the Provisional Government's ministers were meeting. The Kremlin is in Moscow.

questions.content: What did 'dual power' mean in 1917?
options: The Tsar and the Duma ruled together
The Provisional Government had to share authority with the Petrograd Soviet, which influenced soldiers and workers
Russia was ruled jointly with Germany
Bolsheviks and Mensheviks formed one government
questions.explanation: The government had formal authority, but the Soviet's Order No. 1 told soldiers to obey the Soviet where the two conflicted.

questions.content: Why did the decision to continue fighting the First World War damage the Provisional Government?
options: More defeats and shortages followed while the Bolsheviks promised peace
It had to pay reparations to Germany
It lost control of the Winter Palace
It gave the Duma power to appoint generals
questions.explanation: Soldiers and civilians were war-weary. The failed June offensive increased desertions and made the Bolshevik promise of peace popular.

questions.content: A document is dated 24 October 1917 in the Russian (Julian) calendar, which in 1917 was 13 days behind the Western (Gregorian) calendar. What is the matching Western date?
options: 11 October 1917
7 November 1917
24 November 1917
6 November 1917
questions.explanation: Add 13 days: 24 October + 13 days = 6 November. This is why the 'October' Revolution is celebrated in November.

questions.content: How did the Kornilov Affair of August–September 1917 help the Bolsheviks?
options: Kornilov handed power to Lenin
It forced Russia out of the war
Kerensky armed the Red Guards to defend Petrograd, giving the Bolsheviks weapons and credit as defenders of the revolution
It led to the dissolving of the Soviet
questions.explanation: General Kornilov's march on Petrograd failed, but Kerensky's reliance on the Bolsheviks made them stronger and him look weak.

questions.content: Why did peasants lose patience with the Provisional Government on the land question?
options: It gave all land to the Orthodox Church
It delayed land reform until a Constituent Assembly could be elected, so many peasants seized land themselves
It sent the army to collect grain
It abolished private land with no compensation
questions.explanation: The government said it was not legitimate to settle the issue before elections, but peasants wanted land at once.

questions.content: Why did the Bolsheviks gain majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets by autumn 1917?
options: Germany paid workers to vote for them
The Tsar returned to support them
All other parties were banned in September
Their simple promises of peace, land and bread became more popular as the Provisional Government failed to solve problems
questions.explanation: As shortages continued and the war dragged on, more workers and soldiers turned to the party that offered clear answers.

questions.content: An invented letter from a soldier in 1917 says: 'We have no boots, no bread and no wish to fight for the landlords. Whoever offers peace will have our rifles.' What does it suggest?
options: Soldiers' loyalty could go to whichever group promised peace, which weakened the Provisional Government
Soldiers strongly supported Kerensky's offensive
Soldiers wished the Tsar had stayed
The army was well supplied
questions.explanation: The letter shows war-weariness and shortages, and a willingness to support those who offer peace. It is a single voice, so its typicality should be questioned.

questions.content: What happened to the Constituent Assembly elected in November 1917?
options: It became the new government of Russia
It ended the Civil War
It met once in January 1918 and was dissolved by the Bolsheviks
It restored the monarchy
questions.explanation: The Social Revolutionaries won the most seats and the Bolsheviks only about a quarter, so Lenin closed it by force after one day.

questions.content: Which argument best supports the view that October 1917 was a coup rather than a popular revolution?
options: The Bolsheviks had majorities in the main city Soviets
A small, well-organised group took key points with little resistance and later won only about a quarter of the votes in the Constituent Assembly election
Thousands of workers joined the Red Guards
Lenin returned from exile to a large welcome
questions.explanation: The Bolsheviks' limited share of the national vote and the small-scale seizure suggest minority action. The other options support the idea of popular backing.

questions.content: Order No. 1 (March 1917) weakened the Provisional Government because it...
options: ended the war with Germany
made Kerensky commander-in-chief
dissolved the Soviet
told soldiers to obey the Petrograd Soviet's orders where they conflicted with the government's, and created soldiers' committees
questions.explanation: It undermined officers' authority and left the army's loyalty split, which was the heart of dual power.

questions.content: Why could opponents accuse Lenin of being a German agent in 1917?
options: Germany had allowed him to cross its territory in a sealed train in April, hoping he would weaken Russia's war effort
He was born in Berlin
The Bolsheviks signed a treaty with the Kaiser before July
He had commanded a German regiment
questions.explanation: The journey helped Lenin return from Switzerland, and rumours of German money were used against the Bolsheviks after the July Days.

questions.content: Which sequence of events in 1917 is in the correct order?
options: April Theses → Tsar abdicates → Kornilov Affair → Winter Palace stormed
Tsar abdicates → April Theses → Kornilov Affair → Winter Palace stormed
Tsar abdicates → Kornilov Affair → April Theses → Winter Palace stormed
Kornilov Affair → Tsar abdicates → Winter Palace stormed → April Theses
questions.explanation: The Tsar abdicated in March, Lenin issued the April Theses after returning, the Kornilov Affair occurred in late summer, and the Bolsheviks took power in October (Old Style).

questions.content: Which decision most clearly undermined Kerensky's government in summer 1917?
options: Closing the Petrograd Soviet
Ordering the Winter Palace to be abandoned
Inviting Lenin to join the government
Backing a new offensive against Germany that failed with heavy losses
questions.explanation: The June offensive failed, increased desertion and discredited the government with soldiers who wanted peace.

note:
## From autocracy to two revolutions
In 1917 Russia had two revolutions in eight months. Remember that Russia used the Julian calendar, 13 days behind the Western one, until February 1918. Events dated 'February' and 'October' in Russia fall in March and November in the Western calendar.

## The February Revolution
By early 1917 Russia was exhausted by war: millions had been killed or wounded, food and fuel were scarce and prices were rising. On 23 February (Old Style) women workers in Petrograd marked International Women's Day with strikes and bread protests. Within days the strike was general, and soldiers sent to restore order mutinied and joined the crowd. Nicholas II abdicated on 2 March (Old Style); his brother Michael refused the throne, ending the Romanov dynasty.

## Dual power
Two bodies then competed. The **Provisional Government** (first led by Prince Lvov, then by Alexander Kerensky from July) had formal authority but no elected mandate. The **Petrograd Soviet**, a council of workers and soldiers, held real influence over the army. Its **Order No. 1** told soldiers to obey the Soviet if it conflicted with the government. The Provisional Government decided to keep fighting the war, and the failed June offensive caused heavy losses and desertions. It also delayed land reform until a Constituent Assembly was elected, so peasants seized land themselves.

## Lenin and the Bolsheviks
In April Lenin returned from exile in Switzerland, crossing Germany in a sealed train. His **April Theses** rejected cooperation with the Provisional Government and called for 'All power to the Soviets', with the slogan 'Peace, Land and Bread'. The Bolsheviks were blamed for the unrest of the July Days and Lenin fled, but in late August General Kornilov marched troops towards Petrograd. Kerensky armed the Bolshevik Red Guards to defend the city, and the Bolsheviks emerged stronger. By autumn they had majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow Soviets.

## The October Revolution
On 24–25 October (Old Style), which is 6–7 November in the West, Red Guards and soldiers under Trotsky's Military Revolutionary Committee took key points and stormed the Winter Palace with little bloodshed. Lenin formed a government, the Council of People's Commissars. The Constituent Assembly elected in November had a Social Revolutionary majority and the Bolsheviks only about a quarter of seats. It met once, in January 1918, and was then dissolved.

## Common mistakes
- Mixing up the two revolutions: February removed the Tsar, October removed the Provisional Government.
- Saying Lenin personally led the storming of the Winter Palace; Trotsky organised it.
- Giving only one cause. Strong answers combine Provisional Government weaknesses, Bolshevik organisation and slogans, and war-weariness.

## How this is examined
Questions often give a source from 1917, such as a soldier's letter or a poster, and ask you to explain what it shows and why the Bolsheviks won. Another common task asks you to evaluate whether October was a coup or a popular revolution, using evidence on both sides.

Exam tip: when asked to 'evaluate', give a judgement and justify it. For 1917, linking the Provisional Government's failures to the Bolsheviks' promises gives you a clear argument.

flashcards.back: Strikes and bread riots in Petrograd from 23 February (Old Style) 1917; soldiers mutinied and Nicholas II abdicated, ending Romanov rule.
Provisional Government (formal authority) and Petrograd Soviet (influence over workers and soldiers) both held power between March and October 1917.
Soviet order telling soldiers to obey the Soviet where it conflicted with the Provisional Government, undermining officers.
Lenin's programme on returning in April 1917: no support for the Provisional Government, 'All power to the Soviets', 'Peace, Land and Bread'.
August–September 1917: General Kornilov marched on Petrograd. Kerensky armed the Red Guards, which strengthened the Bolsheviks.
Chairman of the Petrograd Soviet who organised the October seizure of power through its Military Revolutionary Committee.
24–25 October (Old Style) = 6–7 November 1917: Bolsheviks took key points and the Winter Palace, overthrowing the Provisional Government.
Elected November 1917. SRs won the most seats, Bolsheviks about a quarter. Met once in January 1918 and was dissolved by the Bolsheviks.
Russia's Julian calendar was 13 days behind the Western Gregorian one in 1917, until Russia switched in February 1918.

subject: history
subTopic: Lenin, Stalin and the Soviet State

questions.content: What did Lenin's New Economic Policy (NEP) of 1921 allow?
options: Full state control of every farm
The return of the Tsar's landlords
Free elections between several parties
Small-scale private trade and peasants selling surplus food after paying a tax
questions.explanation: The NEP replaced grain requisitioning with a tax and allowed limited private business, while the state kept control of major industries.

questions.content: What name was given to Stalin's plans to rapidly build heavy industry from 1928?
options: The New Deal
Five-Year Plans
The Marshall Plan
The Schlieffen Plan
questions.explanation: The first Five-Year Plan began in 1928, setting targets for coal, steel and machinery.

questions.content: What was collectivisation?
options: Giving land to the kulaks
Closing all factories
Combining peasants' individual farms into large, state-controlled collective farms
Moving workers to the countryside
questions.explanation: Under collectivisation from 1929, peasants were pushed to give up private farms and join kolkhozes.

questions.content: Who emerged as the leader of the USSR after the power struggle that followed Lenin's death in 1924?
options: Stalin
Trotsky
Kerensky
Bukharin
questions.explanation: Stalin used his position as General Secretary to defeat his rivals, and Trotsky was exiled in 1929.

questions.content: What were the 'purges' (or Great Terror) of the 1930s?
options: A reform to give workers more rights
A programme to build new cities
An election of new Soviet leaders
Arrests, show trials, executions and imprisonment of real and imagined enemies of Stalin
questions.explanation: Millions were arrested, many sent to the Gulag labour camps or shot, including many Communist Party leaders and army officers.

questions.content: Why did Lenin introduce the NEP in 1921?
options: He wanted to start collectivisation
Germany demanded it in the peace treaty
War Communism had caused famine and unrest, including the Kronstadt mutiny, and he needed to win back the peasants
The Tsar ordered it from exile
questions.explanation: The grain seizures and economic collapse of the Civil War years had made the Bolsheviks unpopular, so Lenin made a strategic retreat.

questions.content: Why did Stalin's regime target the kulaks?
options: They had supported the Tsar's army
They were presented as class enemies who resisted collectivisation, so they were deported, imprisoned or shot
They owned all Soviet factories
They had asked for Five-Year Plans
questions.explanation: 'Dekulakisation' removed better-off peasants and was used to frighten others into joining collective farms.

questions.content: A fictional tractor factory was ordered to produce 40,000 tractors in a year and produced 34,000. What percentage of the target did it reach?
questions.explanation: 34,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.85, or 85%. In reality managers sometimes inflated figures to avoid punishment, which affects how reliable official statistics are.

questions.content: Why did the Soviet regime promote a cult of personality around Stalin?
options: To limit his power
To help the Duma
To prepare for free elections
To build loyalty, present him as an infallible leader and discourage criticism
questions.explanation: Posters, songs and statues showed Stalin as a wise father figure, making opposition seem disloyal.

questions.content: Why were show trials held in the 1930s?
options: To give defendants a fair hearing
To appoint new judges
To produce public confessions that removed rivals and spread fear
To end the Gulag
questions.explanation: Defendants, often old Bolsheviks, were forced to confess to invented crimes, which justified their execution and warned others.

questions.content: An invented poster shows smiling workers beside a gleaming tractor under a bright sun, with a caption praising the Plan. What is it mainly designed to do?
options: Persuade citizens that industrialisation brings prosperity, so it is propaganda not a record of real conditions
Provide an accurate record of living standards
Criticise the Five-Year Plans
Show a foreign view of the USSR
questions.explanation: The poster's purpose is to encourage support and effort, so its cheerful image cannot be taken as evidence of real conditions.

questions.content: Which policy was the main cause of the 1932–33 famine in Ukraine and other grain regions?
options: The NEP
Forced collectivisation with very high grain requisition quotas
German invasion
War Communism
questions.explanation: The state took grain to feed cities and for export, while disruption from collectivisation reduced harvests. Millions died.

questions.content: What did Lenin's 'Testament' (written in 1922–23) say about Stalin?
options: That Stalin should lead the USSR
That Trotsky should be exiled
That the NEP should end
That Stalin was too rude and held too much power as General Secretary and should be removed
questions.explanation: Lenin criticised several leaders and suggested removing Stalin from the post, but Stalin was able to keep his position.

questions.content: Which feature belonged to War Communism (1918–21) but NOT to the NEP?
options: A tax on farmers
Small private businesses
Forced requisitioning of peasants' grain and a ban on private trade
Freedom for peasants to sell surplus
questions.explanation: War Communism meant strict state control to supply the Red Army. The NEP replaced requisitioning with a tax and allowed some trade.

questions.content: Which best explains why Stalin defeated his rivals after Lenin's death?
options: He controlled party appointments as General Secretary, built a network of supporters and played rivals off against each other
He led the Red Army to victory in the Civil War
He had the support of the Duma
He won a national election
questions.explanation: Trotsky was the better-known figure, but Stalin's control of promotions gave him loyal delegates, and he allied with different people at different times.

questions.content: Which statement is the best-balanced judgement on the Five-Year Plans?
options: They were a complete failure
They built heavy industry rapidly, which later helped the war effort, but at a huge human cost with poor quality and neglected consumer goods
They gave workers better lives than in the West
They were abandoned after one year
questions.explanation: Judging the plans requires weighing real industrial growth against forced labour, hardship, falsified figures and shortages of consumer goods.

questions.content: Why did the purge of senior Red Army officers in 1937–38 have long-term consequences?
options: It made the army larger
It made Germany sign a peace treaty
Many experienced commanders were removed, leaving the army less prepared when Germany invaded in 1941
It ended the Gulag
questions.explanation: Losing many senior officers weakened leadership and morale, a factor in the early disasters of 1941.

questions.content: Which feature shows continuity between Tsarist and Stalinist rule?
options: Rule by one leader backed by secret police and censorship, with no free elections
An elected Duma with real power
Private ownership of most land
A free press
questions.explanation: Both regimes used secret police and censorship to control the population, although Stalin's control was far more complete.

note:
## After the Civil War
By 1921 the Bolsheviks had won the Civil War, but Russia was devastated. **War Communism** (1918–21) had meant forced seizure of peasants' grain, state control of industry and bans on private trade. It led to famine, strikes and the Kronstadt naval mutiny in March 1921. Lenin responded with the **New Economic Policy (NEP)**: a grain tax replaced requisitioning, peasants could sell their surplus, and small private businesses were allowed, while the state kept the 'commanding heights' such as heavy industry. Lenin called it a step back to move forward. In 1922 the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) was formed, and Lenin died on 21 January 1924.

## The struggle to succeed Lenin
Stalin was General Secretary of the Communist Party, a post that let him appoint supporters. Trotsky, the hero of the Civil War, was a brilliant speaker but was seen by some as arrogant. Lenin's Testament criticised Stalin, but it was not published. Stalin allied with different rivals in turn and had Trotsky exiled in 1929. Trotsky was murdered in Mexico in 1940.

## Stalin's revolution from above
Stalin ended the NEP. The **Five-Year Plans** (the first began in 1928) set targets for coal, steel, electricity and machinery, run by the planning agency Gosplan. New industrial cities like Magnitogorsk were built, and Soviet industry grew fast. Workers faced long hours, harsh discipline and shortages of consumer goods, and managers sometimes exaggerated results to avoid punishment. In farming, **collectivisation** from 1929 forced peasants into collective farms (kolkhozes). The better-off peasants, called **kulaks**, were labelled class enemies, deported or shot. Grain seizures and disruption helped cause a terrible famine in 1932–33, which killed millions, especially in Ukraine.

## Terror and control
After the murder of the Leningrad party leader Kirov in December 1934, Stalin launched the **Great Terror** (1936–38). Show trials made old Bolshevik leaders confess to invented crimes, and the secret police (NKVD) arrested millions. Many were executed or sent to Gulag labour camps; the officer corps of the Red Army was also purged. Censorship, propaganda and a **cult of personality** presented Stalin as an all-wise father figure. Socialist realism limited artists to approved themes.

## Common mistakes
- Confusing War Communism (forced requisitioning, 1918–21) with the NEP (tax and limited trade, 1921–28).
- Saying the Five-Year Plans were a complete success or a complete failure. Strong answers weigh industrial growth against human cost.
- Treating a poster or official statistic as accurate evidence of conditions.

## How this is examined
Questions often give a propaganda poster, a table of production figures or an official report, and ask you to explain its purpose, evaluate its value and limitation, and use it with your own knowledge to judge the impact of Stalin's policies.

Exam tip: for any source from Soviet authorities, ask who made it, why and for whom. Official figures and posters show what the regime wanted people to believe, so mention their limits as evidence of reality.
